units.sourceHTML: Signature #
units.originalInnerHTML: Signature #

units.sourceHTML: Unlike most other dynamically-typed languages, in Wren a class can have multiple methods with the same name, as long as they have different signatures. The signature includes the method’s name along with the number of arguments it takes. In technical terms, this means you can overload by arity.
units.originalInnerHTML: Unlike most other dynamically-typed languages, in Wren a class can have multiple methods with the same name, as long as they have different signatures. The signature includes the method’s name along with the number of arguments it takes. In technical terms, this means you can overload by arity.

units.sourceHTML: For example, the Random class has two methods for getting a random integer. One takes a minimum and maximum value and returns a value in that range. The other only takes a maximum value and uses 0 as the minimum:
units.originalInnerHTML: For example, the Random class has two methods for getting a random integer. One takes a minimum and maximum value and returns a value in that range. The other only takes a maximum value and uses 0 as the minimum:

units.sourceHTML:
In a language like Python or JavaScript, these would both call a single ⟦CODE0⟧
method, which has some kind of “optional” parameter. The body of the method
figures out how many arguments were passed and uses control flow to handle the
two different behaviors. That means first parameter represents “max unless
another parameter was passed, in which case it’s min”.
units.originalInnerHTML: In a language like Python or JavaScript, these would both call a single int() method, which has some kind of “optional” parameter. The body of the method figures out how many arguments were passed and uses control flow to handle the two different behaviors. That means first parameter represents “max unless another parameter was passed, in which case it’s min”.

units.sourceHTML: This type of ‘variadic’ code isn’t ideal, so Wren doesn’t encourage it.
units.originalInnerHTML: This type of ‘variadic’ code isn’t ideal, so Wren doesn’t encourage it.

units.sourceHTML:
In Wren, these are calls to two entirely separate methods, ⟦CODE0⟧ and
⟦CODE1⟧. This makes it easier to define “overloads” like this since you don’t
need optional parameters or any kind of control flow to handle the different
cases.
units.originalInnerHTML: In Wren, these are calls to two entirely separate methods, int(_,_) and int(_). This makes it easier to define “overloads” like this since you don’t need optional parameters or any kind of control flow to handle the different cases.

units.sourceHTML:
It’s also faster to execute. Since we know how many arguments are passed at
compile time, we can compile this to directly call the right method and avoid
any “if I got two arguments do this…” runtime work.

units.sourceHTML:
Wren has most of the same operators you know and love with the same precedence
and associativity. We have three prefix operators:

units.sourceHTML:
They are just method calls on their operand without any other arguments. An
expression like ⟦CODE0⟧ means “call the ⟦CODE1⟧ method on ⟦CODE2⟧”.
units.originalInnerHTML: They are just method calls on their operand without any other arguments. An expression like !possible means “call the ! method on possible”.

units.sourceHTML:
We also have a slew of infix operators—they have operands on both sides.
They are:
units.originalInnerHTML:

units.sourceHTML:
Like prefix operators, they are all funny ways of writing method calls. The left
operand is the receiver, and the right operand gets passed to it. So ⟦CODE0⟧ is
semantically interpreted as “invoke the ⟦CODE1⟧ method on ⟦CODE2⟧, passing it ⟦CODE3⟧”.
units.originalInnerHTML: Like prefix operators, they are all funny ways of writing method calls. The left operand is the receiver, and the right operand gets passed to it. So a + b is semantically interpreted as “invoke the +(_) method on a, passing it b”.

units.sourceHTML:
Note that ⟦CODE0⟧ is both a prefix and an infix operator. Since they have different
signatures (⟦CODE1⟧ and ⟦CODE2⟧), there’s no ambiguity between them.
units.originalInnerHTML: Note that - is both a prefix and an infix operator. Since they have different signatures (- and -(_)), there’s no ambiguity between them.

units.sourceHTML: Most of these are probably familiar already. The ⟦CODE0⟧ and ⟦CODE1⟧ operators are “range” operators. The number type implements those to create range objects, but they are method calls like other operators.
units.originalInnerHTML: Most of these are probably familiar already. The .. and ... operators are “range” operators. The number type implements those to create range objects, but they are method calls like other operators.

units.sourceHTML: The ⟦CODE0⟧ keyword is a “type test” operator. The base Object class implements it to tell if an object is an instance of a given class. You’ll rarely need to, but you can override ⟦CODE1⟧ in your own classes. That can be useful for things like mocks or proxies where you want an object to masquerade as a certain class.
units.originalInnerHTML: The is keyword is a “type test” operator. The base Object class implements it to tell if an object is an instance of a given class. You’ll rarely need to, but you can override is in your own classes. That can be useful for things like mocks or proxies where you want an object to masquerade as a certain class.
